warmup.q: Thread A only ever writes stats.card. Thread B only ever writes stats.sepa. Both fields are volatile long in the same small object. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing: they never touch the same field, so there's no contention
Lost updates, because ++ on a volatile isn't atomic
Both threads can slow down a lot, because the two fields share a cache line that the cores keep taking from each other
A deadlock between the two threads
warmup.why: Caches move memory in 64-byte lines, and a core that writes a line needs the only copy. Two fields 8 bytes apart sit on one line, so every write by A invalidates B's copy and the other way round. There are no lost updates here: each field has a single writer, so ++ on it is safe.

sections.html:
Your CPU never reads one long from memory. It moves a whole cache line, 64 bytes on x86. The Xeon VM used for this course reports it directly: /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache/index0/coherency_line_size says 64. Each core has its own L1 and L2 caches (small, fast memories right next to the core), and the hardware keeps them coherent, as the memory model track said. Coherent has a price, though. A core that wants to write a line needs the only valid copy of it. Every other core's copy is invalidated, and the next time one of them reads the line, it has to fetch it again.

Now look at what an ordinary object looks like in memory. JOL (Java Object Layout) reads the real field offsets from the running JVM:

Java
static final class Adjacent {
    volatile long card;
    volatile long sepa;
}
// JOL on JDK 21: 32 bytes; card at offset 16, sepa at offset 24
Kotlin
class KAdjacent {
    @Volatile var card = 0L
    @Volatile var sepa = 0L
}
// JOL on JDK 21: 32 bytes; card at offset 16, sepa at offset 24

The first 12 bytes are the object header (an 8-byte mark word and a 4-byte class pointer), then 4 bytes of alignment gap, then the two fields, 8 bytes apart. The whole object is 32 bytes. Unless it happens to straddle a line boundary, both counters live on the same 64-byte line.

For code that reads, that's good news: reading card brings sepa along for free. Arrays of primitives are fast to scan for the same reason. For two threads that each write their own field, it's bad news, and the next section shows why.

Offsets depend on the JVM and its flags. On JDK 25 with -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders (JEP 519) the header shrinks to 8 bytes and card moves to offset 8. JDK 27 turns compact headers on by default (JEP 534). So when you check a layout in a test, check the distance between fields, never absolute offsets.

try.title: Read real layouts with JOL
steps: Run LayoutDemo. Ignore JOL's two # WARNING lines about attaching an agent.
Before reading the output, predict the offset of sepa in each of the three classes.
Look at the last entry: Striped64$Cell, the class LongAdder uses internally. Where is its only field?
Run the Kotlin twin and compare.

code.title: LayoutDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l04; import org.openjdk.jol.info.ClassLayout; /** Prints the real field layout of four classes with JOL: where each field sits, in bytes. */ public class LayoutDemo { static final class Adjacent { volatile long card; volatile long sepa; } static final class PaddedInOneClass { // padding fields between the counters volatile long card; long p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7, p8, p9, p10, p11, p12, p13, p14, p15, p16; volatile long sepa; } static class CardField { volatile long card; } // superclass fields are laid out first static class Pad1 extends CardField { long p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7, p8; } static class SepaField extends Pad1 { volatile long sepa; } static final class Padded extends SepaField { long q1, q2, q3, q4, q5, q6, q7, q8; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { print(Adjacent.class); print(PaddedInOneClass.class); print(Padded.class); // the cell behind LongAdder: the JDK pads it with @Contended print(Class.forName("java.util.concurrent.atomic.Striped64$Cell")); } static void print(Class<?> type) { ClassLayout layout = ClassLayout.parseClass(type); System.out.println(type.getSimpleName() + ": " + layout.instanceSize() + " bytes"); layout.fields().stream() .filter(f -> f.name().equals("card") || f.name().equals("sepa") || f.name().equals("value")) .forEach(f -> System.out.printf(" %-5s at offset %3d%n", f.name(), f.offset())); } }

try.expect: On JDK 21: Adjacent is 32 bytes with card at 16 and sepa at 24. PaddedInOneClass is 160 bytes with sepa at 152. Padded, built from a class hierarchy, is 160 bytes with sepa at 88, 72 bytes after card. Cell is 152 bytes, and its value field sits at offset 144: the JDK pads it on purpose. Kotlin's @Volatile var fields get exactly the same layout. On JDK 25 JOL also prints warnings about sun.misc.Unsafe, which it uses internally.

sections.h: False sharing: two threads, two fields, one line
sections.html:
Put a thread on each counter. The card thread only writes card, the SEPA thread only writes sepa. They share no data, so there is nothing to lock and no race. But they share a line. Each write by core 1 invalidates core 2's copy of the line, and core 2's next write has to take the line back. The line bounces between the cores on almost every write. This is false sharing: the program shares nothing, the hardware shares a lot.

FalseSharingDemo runs exactly that, 25 million increments per thread, first with the adjacent fields and then with the fields padded apart. On the shared 4-vCPU VM used for this course, one run printed this:

round 1: adjacent 1,220 ms   padded   247 ms
round 2: adjacent   957 ms   padded   225 ms
round 3: adjacent 1,387 ms   padded   206 ms

That's a clear gap. Here's the honest part, though. An earlier, more careful experiment on the same VM, with JMH running two threads per group, could not show any false-sharing effect: the error bars of padded and unpadded overlapped, and a second run reversed the order of the first. The Kotlin twin, run a few minutes after the Java one, showed a much smaller gap in one round. Whether you see the effect depends on whether your two threads land on different physical cores, on the CPU, and on what else the machine is doing. Two threads on hyperthreads (two hardware threads that share one physical core) share that core's L1 and L2, so there's no line to bounce.

So don't promise anyone a speed-up from padding. The mechanism is certain, the size of the effect isn't, and the only way to know is to measure on the hardware you run on. When it does hit, it hits code that looks perfectly innocent: per-partition counters in a Kafka consumer, a stats object with one field per worker thread, an array of per-thread totals where the slots sit 8 bytes apart.

try.title: Race two counters on one line
steps: Read FalseSharingDemo. Predict: will the adjacent run be slower, the same, or faster than the padded one on your machine?
Run it, then run it again. Then run the Kotlin twin.
If you see a big gap, check how many physical cores your machine has (lscpu on Linux, sysctl -n hw.physicalcpu on macOS).

code.title: FalseSharingDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l04; /** * Two threads, each incrementing its OWN volatile counter 25 million times. * Run 1: the two counters sit next to each other. Run 2: they are padded apart. * Whether you see a difference depends on your CPU and where the OS puts the threads. */ public class FalseSharingDemo { // the two counters in one 32-byte object: almost certainly on the same 64-byte cache line static final class Adjacent { volatile long card; volatile long sepa; } // superclass fields come first, so the padding class sits between card and sepa static class CardField { volatile long card; } static class Pad1 extends CardField { long p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7, p8; } static class SepaField extends Pad1 { volatile long sepa; } static final class Padded extends SepaField { long q1, q2, q3, q4, q5, q6, q7, q8; } static final int N = 25_000_000; static long run(Runnable a, Runnable b) throws InterruptedException { Thread t1 = new Thread(a), t2 = new Thread(b); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); t1.start(); t2.start(); t1.join(); t2.join(); return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int round = 1; round <= 3; round++) { Adjacent adj = new Adjacent(); long msAdjacent = run(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) adj.card++; }, () -> { for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) adj.sepa++; }); Padded pad = new Padded(); long msPadded = run(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) pad.card++; }, () -> { for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) pad.sepa++; }); System.out.printf("round %d: adjacent %,5d ms padded %,5d ms (counts %d/%d, %d/%d)%n", round, msAdjacent, msPadded, adj.card, adj.sepa, pad.card, pad.sepa); } } }

alt.title: FalseSharingDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l04 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Kotlin twin of FalseSharingDemo.java: two threads, each incrementing its OWN volatile counter. // Run 1: the counters sit next to each other. Run 2: they are padded apart (KPadded from LayoutDemo.kt). // Whether you see a difference depends on your CPU and where the OS puts the threads. private const val N = 25_000_000 private fun timeTwo(a: () -> Unit, b: () -> Unit): Long { val t0 = System.nanoTime() val t1 = thread { a() } val t2 = thread { b() } t1.join(); t2.join() return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 } fun main() { for (round in 1..3) { val adj = KAdjacent() val msAdjacent = timeTwo({ repeat(N) { adj.card++ } }, { repeat(N) { adj.sepa++ } }) val pad = KPadded() val msPadded = timeTwo({ repeat(N) { pad.card++ } }, { repeat(N) { pad.sepa++ } }) println("round %d: adjacent %,5d ms padded %,5d ms (counts %d/%d, %d/%d)" .format(round, msAdjacent, msPadded, adj.card, adj.sepa, pad.card, pad.sepa)) } }

try.expect: On many laptops with several physical cores, the adjacent run is several times slower than the padded one, as in the run above. You may also see a small gap or none, depending on the CPU and where the scheduler puts the threads. All four counts always end at exactly 25,000,000: false sharing costs time, never correctness.

sections.h: Padding pushes hot fields onto separate lines
sections.html:
The fix is to keep at least 64 bytes between fields that different threads write. There are three ways, from least to most trustworthy.

Padding fields in one class: put 8 or more unused longs between card and sepa. On today's HotSpot it works (sepa moved to offset 152), but JMH's false-sharing sample warns that this is "not versatile because JVMs can freely rearrange the field order, even of the same type".

A class hierarchy: the same sample notes that "superclass fields are usually laid out first". So put each hot field and each block of padding in its own class, and chain them:

Java
abstract class CardCounter { volatile long card; }
abstract class PadAfterCard extends CardCounter { long p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7, p8; }
abstract class SepaCounter extends PadAfterCard { volatile long sepa; }

public final class SettlementCounters extends SepaCounter {
    public void addCard() { card++; }      // only the card thread calls this
    public void addSepa() { sepa++; }      // only the SEPA thread calls this
}
Kotlin
abstract class CardCounter { @Volatile @JvmField var card = 0L }
abstract class PadAfterCard : CardCounter() {
    @JvmField var p1 = 0L; @JvmField var p2 = 0L; @JvmField var p3 = 0L; @JvmField var p4 = 0L
    @JvmField var p5 = 0L; @JvmField var p6 = 0L; @JvmField var p7 = 0L; @JvmField var p8 = 0L
}
abstract class SepaCounter : PadAfterCard() { @Volatile @JvmField var sepa = 0L }

class SettlementCounters : SepaCounter() {
    fun addCard() { card++ }               // only the card thread calls this
    fun addSepa() { sepa++ }               // only the SEPA thread calls this
}

This is what the lab asks for. @JvmField in the Kotlin version makes each property a plain public field, which keeps the layout obvious.

@Contended: the JDK's own annotation, jdk.internal.vm.annotation.Contended, available since JDK 8. The JVM adds ContendedPaddingWidth bytes of padding, 128 by default, around each annotated field. JOL on a class with both fields annotated shows card at offset 144, sepa at 280, and a 288-byte object. Its Javadoc warns that it "will nearly always add significant space overhead to objects". There are two catches for your own classes. The JVM ignores the annotation outside the JDK unless you run with -XX:-RestrictContended: without the flag, JOL shows the same 16 and 24 as no annotation at all, with no warning. And it lives in an internal package, so compiling needs --add-exports java.base/jdk.internal.vm.annotation=ALL-UNNAMED. javac refuses that together with --release, with "exporting a package from system module java.base is not allowed with --release", so this course's labs, which compile with --release 21, can't use it.

Every padding costs memory: 160 bytes instead of 32 here, and 288 with @Contended. That's nothing for one counter object and a lot for a million of them. Pad the few objects that several threads write in a hot loop, and nothing else.

Check yourself: a class declares volatile long a;, then seven padding longs, then volatile long b;. JOL shows a at 16 and b at 80. Can they share a line? (No: 64 bytes apart. But another JVM may order the fields differently, which is why the lab's test reads the real offsets instead of trusting the source.)

sections.h: LongAdder is the padding you should actually use
sections.html:
Hand padding is for library authors. For a counter in your service, the JDK already did the work. LongAdder (and LongAccumulator) extend Striped64, whose source explains the design: table entries are a "variant of AtomicLong padded (via @Contended) to reduce cache contention", because "Atomic objects residing in arrays will tend to be placed adjacent to each other, and so will most often share cache lines (with a huge negative performance impact) without this precaution". That's the value at offset 144 you saw in LayoutDemo.

The cells are lazy. "When there is no contention, all updates are made to the base field." On the first failed compare-and-set, the table is created with 2 cells, and it doubles under more contention. Each thread then mostly updates its own cell, on its own cache line. sum() adds the base and the cells. As "Atomics and compare-and-set" said, sum() is not an atomic snapshot, so use LongAdder for counters you read now and then, such as metrics, and AtomicLong when the value drives a decision.

Java
public final class RequestMetrics {
    private final LongAdder count = new LongAdder();
    private final LongAdder totalCents = new LongAdder();

    public void record(long amountCents) {   // called by every request thread
        count.increment();
        totalCents.add(amountCents);
    }

    public long count() { return count.sum(); }   // read by the metrics scraper
}
Kotlin
class RequestMetrics {
    private val count = LongAdder()
    private val totalCents = LongAdder()

    fun record(amountCents: Long) {          // called by every request thread
        count.increment()
        totalCents.add(amountCents)
    }

    fun count(): Long = count.sum()          // read by the metrics scraper
}

AdderDemo shows the difference with four threads counting 10 million requests each. In one run on the course VM, AtomicLong took 640 to 760 ms per round and LongAdder about 200 ms. With an AtomicLong, all four cores fight over one line, and every failed compare-and-set retries. With a LongAdder, each core mostly works on its own padded cell. Like the false-sharing demo, the gap depends on the machine, and the Kotlin twin's run here showed a smaller one.

try.title: AtomicLong against LongAdder
steps: Predict which one finishes first with four threads, and by how much.
Change THREADS to 1 and run again. Does LongAdder still win?

code.title: AdderDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l04; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** Four threads count 10 million requests each, into one AtomicLong and then into one LongAdder. */ public class AdderDemo { static final int THREADS = 4, PER_THREAD = 10_000_000; static long time(Runnable perThread) throws InterruptedException { CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] ts = new Thread[THREADS]; for (int i = 0; i < THREADS; i++) { ts[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } perThread.run(); }); ts[i].start(); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); go.countDown(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int round = 1; round <= 3; round++) { AtomicLong atomic = new AtomicLong(); long msAtomic = time(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < PER_THREAD; i++) atomic.incrementAndGet(); }); LongAdder adder = new LongAdder(); long msAdder = time(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < PER_THREAD; i++) adder.increment(); }); System.out.printf("round %d: AtomicLong %,5d ms (%,d) LongAdder %,5d ms (%,d)%n", round, msAtomic, atomic.get(), msAdder, adder.sum()); } } }

alt.title: AdderDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l04 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Kotlin twin of AdderDemo.java: four threads count 10 million requests each, // into one AtomicLong and then into one LongAdder. private const val THREADS = 4 private const val PER_THREAD = 10_000_000 private fun timeAll(perThread: () -> Unit): Long { val go = CountDownLatch(1) val ts = List(THREADS) { thread { go.await(); perThread() } } val t0 = System.nanoTime() go.countDown() ts.forEach { it.join() } return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 } fun main() { for (round in 1..3) { val atomic = AtomicLong() val msAtomic = timeAll { repeat(PER_THREAD) { atomic.incrementAndGet() } } val adder = LongAdder() val msAdder = timeAll { repeat(PER_THREAD) { adder.increment() } } println("round %d: AtomicLong %,5d ms (%,d) LongAdder %,5d ms (%,d)" .format(round, msAtomic, atomic.get(), msAdder, adder.sum())) } }

try.expect: With four threads, LongAdder is usually clearly faster, and both always count exactly 40,000,000. With one thread, AtomicLong was faster on the course VM (about 70 ms against 110 ms). With no contention, LongAdder only touches its base field, its cells never exist, and its extra checks are pure cost.

analogy: Two cashiers share one cash drawer. Each keeps their own money in their own compartment, so they never take each other's coins. But only one of them can have the drawer open at a time, so each sale waits for the other cashier to close it. That is false sharing: separate data, one physical unit. Padding gives each cashier their own drawer. LongAdder is the store manager's solution: one drawer per cashier, added up at closing time. The analogy breaks on timing: a cashier waits seconds, while a core waits for a line transfer measured in nanoseconds, so you only notice it when it happens hundreds of millions of times.
world: Look for objects that several threads write in a tight loop: a stats object with one counter per Kafka partition, an array of per-worker totals in a batch settlement job, hand-rolled request counters in a Quarkus filter. For metrics, use LongAdder (or a metrics library) instead of AtomicLong or a volatile field: it's correct under contention and pads its own cells. Reach for manual padding only when a profile or a JMH run on your production hardware shows the cost, and then pad the one or two objects involved, not every class. Remember too that object layouts change with the JDK: compact object headers are on by default in JDK 27.
mistake:
The common mistake is fixing a "slow counter" by making each thread write its own slot of a plain array, believing that no sharing means no contention. The slots are 8 bytes apart, so eight of them share one line, and the threads still fight over it. The other common mistake is padding with unused fields and never checking the result: the JVM may move fields, and an unused field doesn't stop it. Check with JOL, measure with a forked benchmark, or use LongAdder, which does both for you.

Java
long[] perThread = new long[8];          // 8 slots, one 64-byte line
perThread[workerId]++;                   // every worker writes the same line
Kotlin
val perThread = LongArray(8)             // 8 slots, one 64-byte line
perThread[workerId]++                    // every worker writes the same line

kotlin.html: abstract class CardCounter { @Volatile @JvmField var card = 0L } abstract class PadAfterCard : CardCounter() { @JvmField var p1 = 0L; @JvmField var p2 = 0L; @JvmField var p3 = 0L; @JvmField var p4 = 0L @JvmField var p5 = 0L; @JvmField var p6 = 0L; @JvmField var p7 = 0L; @JvmField var p8 = 0L } abstract class SepaCounter : PadAfterCard() { @Volatile @JvmField var sepa = 0L } class SettlementCounters : SepaCounter() { fun addCard() { card++ } // only the card thread calls this fun addSepa() { sepa++ } // only the SEPA thread calls this }

compare.note: Both compile to the same JVM classes with the same field layout, because layout is decided by the JVM, not the language. The differences are in what you write. Kotlin classes are final by default, so the padding classes need abstract or open. A Kotlin var property is a private field plus a getter and setter; @JvmField exposes the field directly, and @Volatile makes it volatile. In both languages the padding fields are never read, and nothing in the language guarantees the order of fields within one class, which is why the hierarchy is the safer trick.

worked.title: Find false sharing in a stats object and fix it

steps.say: A Kafka consumer has two partition threads. Each updates its own counters in one shared stats object. Profiling shows both threads spending time in record, which does almost nothing. Start by printing the layout.
steps.code: System.out.println(ClassLayout.parseClass(PartitionStats.class).toPrintable());

steps.say: The two hot fields are 8 bytes apart. Thread 0 writes p0Processed, thread 1 writes p1Processed, and both sit on one line.

steps.say: Give each partition its own object instead of padding one. Two PartitionCounter objects allocated one after the other can still end up next to each other in memory, so if the profile still shows the problem, pad the counter class or use a LongAdder per field. Self-check: why don't separate objects guarantee separate lines? (Answer: the allocator places new objects next to each other in the thread's allocation buffer, so two small objects created together are often only a few bytes apart.)
steps.code: final class PartitionCounter { volatile long processed; // one writer: the partition's own thread } PartitionCounter[] counters = { new PartitionCounter(), new PartitionCounter() };

steps.say: Verify with a forked JMH benchmark using two threads, on the hardware you deploy to, not on your laptop alone. Keep the version that measures faster there. If neither is clearly faster, keep the simpler code.

lab.title: Pad two counters and fix a metrics counter
steps: Run the tests. Three of four fail: card and sepa are 8 bytes apart (at 16 and 24), and RequestMetrics loses updates when 8 threads record at once.
Lay out SettlementCounters so card and sepa are at least 64 bytes apart. Keep both fields volatile long with those exact names, and keep the public methods. A chain of classes is the reliable way.
Fix RequestMetrics so count() and totalCents() are exact under contention. Writes happen on every request and reads every few seconds, so pick the tool built for that.
Run the tests until all four pass. Run them twice: the metrics test is a race test.
Optional: print ClassLayout.parseClass(SettlementCounters.class).toPrintable() in a scratch test and look at your layout.
hints: HotSpot lays out superclass fields before subclass fields. abstract class CardCounter { volatile long card; }, then a class with eight long padding fields extending it, then a class with sepa extending that, then SettlementCounters at the end of the chain.
The fields in the superclasses can't be private if SettlementCounters needs to read them. Package-private works, and JOL finds fields in superclasses too.

count++ on a volatile is a read and a write, so two threads can both read 41 and both write 42. With many writers, LongAdder.increment() and add(amount) are exact and spread the writes over padded cells.
The reference solution puts sepa 72 bytes after card and passes on JDK 21 and 25.
lab.done: All four tests in CacheLineTest pass, twice in a row.

drill.title: Explain a layout and write the fix from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. JOL prints card at offset 16 and sepa at offset 24 for a class that two threads write. Write two sentences on what goes wrong and why, then write a padded version using a class chain. Then write the one-line answer you'd give for a request counter written by 200 threads.

answer.html: // card and sepa are 8 bytes apart, so they share one 64-byte cache line. Each write by one // core invalidates the other core's copy, so the line bounces between them (false sharing). abstract class CardCounter { volatile long card; } abstract class PadAfterCard extends CardCounter { long p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7, p8; } abstract class SepaCounter extends PadAfterCard { volatile long sepa; } public final class SettlementCounters extends SepaCounter { } // 200 writers, occasional reads: use a LongAdder private final LongAdder requests = new LongAdder();

Each write by one // core invalidates the other core's copy, so the line bounces between them (false sharing). abstract class CardCounter { @Volatile @JvmField var card = 0L } abstract class PadAfterCard : CardCounter() { @JvmField var p1 = 0L; @JvmField var p2 = 0L; @JvmField var p3 = 0L; @JvmField var p4 = 0L @JvmField var p5 = 0L; @JvmField var p6 = 0L; @JvmField var p7 = 0L; @JvmField var p8 = 0L } abstract class SepaCounter : PadAfterCard() { @Volatile @JvmField var sepa = 0L } class SettlementCounters : SepaCounter() // 200 writers, occasional reads: use a LongAdder private val requests = LongAdder()

recap: Caches move memory in 64-byte lines, and a core that writes a line invalidates every other core's copy.
False sharing: two threads writing different fields on the same line make it bounce between cores. It costs time, never correctness, and how much depends on the hardware.
Pad hot fields at least 64 bytes apart. A class hierarchy is reliable; padding fields in one class may be reordered; @Contended needs -XX:-RestrictContended and internal exports for your own classes.
Check layouts with JOL and assert distances, not offsets: headers differ between JDKs (compact headers are default in JDK 27).
For counters in application code, use LongAdder: its cells are padded with @Contended and only created under contention.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why giving each consumer thread its own field in a shared stats object didn't make the counters fast, and what you'd do instead.
explain.answer: The fields are separate, so there's no race, but they sit 8 bytes apart, which puts them on the same 64-byte cache line. A core can only write a line it owns exclusively, so each write by one thread invalidates the other core's copy and the line moves back and forth on almost every update. That's false sharing. One fix is to pad the fields at least 64 bytes apart, ideally with a class hierarchy since the JVM may reorder fields within one class, and to check the offsets with JOL. For ordinary counters I'd use a LongAdder per counter instead: it creates padded cells only when threads contend and adds them up when we read. And I'd only believe a speed-up after measuring it on our real hardware, because how much false sharing costs depends on the CPU and where the threads run.

deeper.html:
JMH protects you from one source of false sharing automatically. Its false-sharing sample says "@States are automatically padded", but "This padding does not extend to the State internals". Fields inside your @State object can still share a line, which is exactly what that sample demonstrates with several techniques side by side. To measure it on your own hardware, run that sample with several forks on a machine with real cores, and pin the threads to different physical cores if you can.

Why does the JDK pad with 128 bytes when lines are 64? The flag ContendedPaddingWidth says how many bytes to pad, nothing more. A common explanation is that some CPUs prefetch the neighbouring line too, so a 64-byte gap can still let two hot fields interfere. That explanation isn't something this course could check against a primary source, so treat 128 as "the JDK's safe default" rather than a rule.

Two other tools look at the same problem from the hardware side. perf c2c on Linux reports cache lines that bounce between cores (JMH wraps it as -prof perfc2c). And a CPU profiler such as async-profiler, in lesson 6, shows the symptom: lots of samples on a trivial line such as count++.

There's also true sharing, which padding can't fix: many threads writing the same field, like an AtomicLong hit by every request. The only fixes there are to write less often or to split the value, which is what LongAdder does.
